title: Obedience Is Better Than Sacrifice: Saul Rejected
summary: Samuel sends Saul to carry out the LORD's judgment on the Amalekites, but Saul spares King Agag and the best of the livestock. When Samuel confronts him, Saul insists he has obeyed and blames the troops, and Samuel declares that obedience is better than sacrifice and that the LORD has rejected Saul as king. Saul's grip tears Samuel's robe, a sign that the kingdom has been torn from him and given to a better man. Samuel executes Agag and never visits Saul again, though he mourns for him.
story: This is the turning point of Saul's story. In chapter 13 Samuel announced that Saul's dynasty would not endure; here the LORD rejects Saul himself as king. From this chapter on, Saul remains on the throne in name, but the story's attention and God's favor move to the young man anointed in chapter 16. The chapter also reaches back to Israel's beginnings: Amalek attacked Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 17:8-16), and Deuteronomy 25:17-19 charged Israel to remember and to blot out Amalek's memory once they had rest in the land. Saul is given that old unfinished task and does not finish it.
historical:
The Amalekites were a nomadic or semi-nomadic people of the Negev and the Sinai, the dry lands south of Judah, known in the Old Testament mainly as raiders. They appear repeatedly as Israel's enemies, from the wilderness period through the time of the judges (Judges 6:3) and into David's day, when an Amalekite band burns Ziklag (chapter 30), which shows that Saul's campaign did not end them. Havilah and Shur mark a broad desert region toward Egypt; their exact locations are uncertain. The Carmel of verse 12 is a town in the hill country of Judah, south of Hebron, not the famous Mount Carmel on the northern coast.

The army figures in verse 4 are large for this period, and some scholars think the Hebrew word usually translated thousand could also mean a military unit or clan contingent, which would give much smaller numbers. Others take the numbers as they stand. Later Jewish tradition connected Agag with Haman, called “the Agagite” in Esther 3:1, the man who tried to destroy the Jews in Persia centuries later.
cultural:
To “devote to destruction” translates a single Hebrew verb for the ban (herem), a practice in which people or goods were given over entirely to God and therefore could not be kept for human use. In warfare this meant total destruction, with no plunder taken. A similar practice is known outside Israel: the Moabite king Mesha, in an inscription from the ninth century BC (the Mesha Stele), boasts of devoting an Israelite town to his god Chemosh. Under the ban, keeping the best animals was not a lesser obedience but a theft from God, which is why Achan's hidden plunder was so serious in Joshua 7.

Saul's monument at Carmel (verse 12) was a victory marker, the kind of memorial kings erected to themselves. The robe torn in verse 27 carries symbolic weight: a garment could stand for a person's status and authority, and tearing it could enact a verdict (compare the prophet Ahijah tearing his cloak before Jeroboam in 1 Kings 11:29-31). Grabbing the hem of a robe was also a gesture of pleading. Samuel's execution of Agag “before the LORD at Gilgal” is presented as the carrying out of God's sentence that Saul left undone.
literary: The chapter is a prophetic judgment story built around a confrontation. The command (verses 1 to 3) is precise, and the account of Saul's action (verses 7 to 9) is precise about what he did not do. The Hebrew verb for hearing or obeying (shama) runs through the chapter: Saul is told to listen (verse 1), fails to obey (verse 19), and finally admits he feared the people and obeyed their voice (verse 24). Samuel's reply in verses 22 and 23 breaks into poetry, and it states the moral of the story in parallel lines. The chapter is framed by the LORD's regret (verses 11 and 35), with Samuel's statement that God does not change his mind (verse 29) set in the middle, a deliberate tension the narrator leaves for the reader to hold.

outline.t: Saul's campaign: Agag and the best spared
The LORD regrets making Saul king
Samuel confronts Saul, who claims he obeyed
Saul's confession, the torn robe, and the torn kingdom
Agag's death and the final parting of Samuel and Saul

doctrines.note: What was devoted to God belonged to God alone. Saul treated the LORD's judgment as an opportunity for plunder dressed up as worship. Holiness means God's claims are not negotiable, even when the negotiation is framed as sacrifice.

Saul says “I have sinned” twice, but his confession blames the people, asks at once to be honored before the elders, and centers on his position. The chapter distinguishes regret over consequences from repentance that turns toward God, as Psalm 51 later shows from David's side.

God is said to regret, and also not to change his mind like a human being. Taken together, these show that God truly responds to human actions, while his character and purposes are not fickle or capricious as a man's are.

The judgment on Amalek is presented as God's delayed response to Amalek's attack on Israel in the wilderness, and the judgment on Saul as the response to his disobedience. In both cases the narrator insists that God's justice is patient but not endlessly deferred.

words.note: Charam, to devote to destruction. It means to set something wholly apart for God, so that it cannot be used by people, which in war meant utter destruction. The noun form (herem) is the ban. The word appears seven times in this chapter, which shows how central the ban is to Saul's failure.

Nacham, to regret or relent. The LORD “regretted” making Saul king (verses 11 and 35), yet he “does not lie or change His mind” (verse 29). Theologians read this in different ways, but most agree that the first describes God's real grief and response to human sin, while the second denies that God changes his purposes the way people do.

Ma'as, to reject. The chapter's verdict rests on a matched pair: Saul rejected the word of the LORD, so the LORD rejected him as king. The same verb described Israel's rejection of the LORD as king in 8:7. Rejection answers rejection.

Teraphim, household idols, rendered “idolatry” in verse 23. These were small figures used in homes, sometimes for divination (Genesis 31:19; Judges 17:5). Samuel's point is that stubborn self-will is as serious in God's eyes as the pagan practices Israel despised.

christ: Samuel's saying that “obedience is better than sacrifice” becomes a theme of the prophets (Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6-8), and Jesus twice quotes Hosea's version to confront religion that keeps rituals and neglects mercy (Matthew 9:13; 12:7). The letter to the Hebrews applies Psalm 40 to Christ, the one who came to do God's will rather than simply offer sacrifices, and whose obedient self-offering is the one sacrifice that finally deals with sin (Hebrews 10:5-10). Saul, the king who would not obey, is the dark background for the King who obeyed to the point of death. The link is a biblical theme traced across the canon, not a hidden prediction in this chapter.

hard.q: How can God command the destruction of an entire people, including children and infants?
hard.a: This is one of the hardest passages in the Old Testament, and it should not be softened. Christians have answered in several ways. Some stress that the command is a unique act of divine judgment on a people with a long record of predatory violence, issued by the Creator who alone has the right to give and take life, and never a general license for Israel or anyone else. Some scholars argue that the language of total destruction is partly stylized war rhetoric, common in ancient Near Eastern records, since Amalekites reappear a few chapters later (27:8; 30:1); others reply that the text still presents the command as total and must be faced on those terms. Others read these texts as part of a progressive revelation that culminates in Christ's command to love enemies, while still affirming God's justice. Whatever view one takes, the New Testament does not repeat such commands, and Jesus forbids his followers to take up the sword to advance his kingdom. The chapter itself does not celebrate slaughter; it is about whether God's king will obey God, and its closing note is grief.

questions: Saul kept the best and called it a sacrifice. Where might you offer God religious activity in place of the obedience he actually asked for?
Saul admitted he “feared the people.” How does the fear of others' opinion shape your choices?
Compare Saul's two confessions with a confession that seeks God rather than reputation. What marks the difference?
